content: 1. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is a form of tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that are resistant to at least both rifampicin and isoniazid, the two most potent first-line anti-TB drugs. 2. People-centered services adopt a human rights-based approach to healthcare, integrating the perspectives of individuals, caregivers, families, and communities as active participants and beneficiaries of trusted health systems. These systems are designed to address the comprehensive needs of people rather than focusing solely on individual diseases, while also respecting social preferences. 3. The term people who use drugs refers to individuals who consume psychoactive substances through various routes, including injection, oral, inhalation, transmucosal, or transdermal methods. This definition excludes the use of widely consumed substances such as tobacco, alcohol, caffeine-containing beverages, and foods. 4. A person with presumptive TB is someone exhibiting symptoms or signs suggestive of tuberculosis disease. This term replaces the previously used TB suspect. 5. Tuberculosis disease refers to the clinical state caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this document, it is often referred to as TB disease or active TB to distinguish it from TB infection. 6. TB infection is characterized by a persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically active TB disease. Most infected individuals show no symptoms but remain at risk of developing TB disease. This condition was previously termed latent TB infection (LTBI), but the term TB infection (TBI) is now preferred, as not all infections can be considered latent. 7. There is no definitive test for directly identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in humans. 8. TB preventive treatment (TPT) is offered to individuals at risk of developing TB disease to reduce that risk. It is also referred to as treatment of TB infection, LTBI treatment, or TB preventive therapy. 9. Universal health coverage ensures that individuals and communities have access to high-quality essential health services, including promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care, without experiencing financial hardship. 10. The terms breastfeeding, pregnant, or postpartum women are used to describe individuals in these categories, as most data are disaggregated by sex rather than gender identity. The term woman is intended to include all individuals who identify as women and/or have the capacity to give birth, including transgender men and other gender-diverse individuals with reproductive capacity. 11. People living with HIV are approximately 14 times more likely to develop TB disease, experience poorer treatment outcomes, and have more than double the mortality rate during TB treatment compared to the general population diagnosed with TB. 12. Addressing HIV-associated TB through integrated, patient-centered care and prevention is a critical component of the WHO End TB Strategy. 13. WHO has issued recommendations for screening, diagnosing, treating, caring for, and preventing HIV-associated TB for several decades. These guidelines aim to reduce the burden of HIV-associated TB in populations at risk or affected by both diseases. 14. Despite significant progress in scaling up collaborative TB/HIV activities and advances in TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, TB remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV globally. Gaps persist in the implementation of TB/HIV collaborative activities. 15. Since 2012, WHO has updated several recommendations and introduced new ones as evidence has evolved. These recommendations are consolidated in the WHO guidelines on TB and HIV-associated TB. 16. The WHO TB/HIV guidelines include 31 specific recommendations on HIV-associated TB, accompanied by operational guidance and implementation considerations. 17. Recommendations specific to HIV-associated TB in children and adolescents are detailed in the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB, Module 5: Management of TB in Children and Adolescents. 18. WHO recommendations on TB screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care for all individuals with TB, regardless of HIV status, are available in the respective modules of the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB. 19. WHO provides recommendations to reduce the burden of TB among people living with HIV and vice versa, aiming to address the dual burden of these diseases effectively. 20. People living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB disease at every visit to a healthcare facility. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 21. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, systematic TB screening should use the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats). Those reporting any of these symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 22. C-reactive protein (CRP) testing with a cutoff of >5 mg/L may be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 23. Chest X-rays may be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 24. In populations where TB screening is recommended, computer-aided detection software may replace human readers for interpreting digital chest X-rays for TB screening and triage. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 25. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests may be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 26. In inpatient settings with a TB prevalence >10%, HIV-positive adults and adolescents should be systematically tested for TB disease using molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 27. For diagnosing disseminated TB in HIV-positive individuals, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used in blood as an initial diagnostic test. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 28. Lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing is strongly recommended to assist in diagnosing active TB in HIV-positive individuals with TB symptoms, advanced HIV disease, or a CD4 count <200 cells/mm³ in inpatient settings. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 29. In outpatient settings, LF-LAM testing is suggested for HIV-positive individuals with TB symptoms or a CD4 count <100 cells/mm³. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 30. WHO recommends against using LF-LAM testing in HIV-positive individuals without TB symptoms or with a CD4 count ≥200 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 31. TB patients living with HIV should receive at least the same duration of daily TB treatment as HIV-negative TB patients. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty of evidence. 32. HIV-positive individuals with TB and histoplasmosis coinfection should receive TB therapy according to WHO treatment guidelines. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 33. In high HIV and TB burden settings, TB treatment may be provided in HIV care settings where a TB diagnosis has been made. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 34. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes those on antiretroviral therapy, pregnant women, and individuals previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or availability of LTBI testing. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty of evidence. 35. Clinical algorithms should be used to rule out active TB before offering TB preventive treatment to adults and adolescents living with HIV. Those reporting symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. Preventive treatment should be offered if active TB is excluded. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 36. Chest radiography may be offered to people living with HIV on ART, and preventive treatment should be given to those with no abnormal radiographic findings. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 37. Either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) can be used to test for TB infection. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 38. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) may be used to test for TB infection. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 39. Recommended regimens for LTBI treatment include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. A 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone may also be offered as alternatives. These are strong recommendations with moderate to high certainty of evidence. 40. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV with unknown or positive LTBI test results and unlikely to have active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT). This should be provided regardless of ART status, immunosuppression level, previous TB treatment history, or pregnancy. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 41. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation with low quality of evidence. 42. All household contacts of individuals with HIV-associated TB should be offered HIV testing services. This is a strong recommendation with very low quality of evidence. 43. In high HIV burden settings, all household and close contacts of people with TB should be offered HIV testing services. This is a strong recommendation with very low quality of evidence. 44. In low HIV burden settings, household members and close contacts of people with TB who exhibit symptoms compatible with TB disease may be offered HIV testing services as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation with very low quality of evidence. 45. Partner services should be offered to individuals with HIV-associated TB. This is a strong recommendation with moderate quality of evidence. 46. A comprehensive package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support, should be offered to everyone presenting with advanced HIV disease. This is a strong recommendation with moderate quality of evidence.
